p: On the Sunday morning after, Kit opened the log Vern had handed her unasked in the heritage room. It was from March 2001. His Doppler had quit, and he'd worked a crosswind by hand: a right triangle of five hundred, a hundred forty and four eighty. The last line said he'd pointed the jet sixteen degrees left to go straight. He'd pointed into the thing pushing him, and Kit had spent seven years pointing away from hers.

At his kitchen table Vern handed her four sets of math problems. She ran each one on the egg timer at the real test's twenty two minutes, then went back over her misses slowly. He showed her how he'd factored at the nav table, with the pairs written down the margin of the log.
At the water plant she read the backup generator's tank chart, worked out what the full tank held, and ordered diesel.

On a Saturday in the heritage room, Corbin Haas brought back an old altimeter he'd fixed for the display case. He told her the first week of pilot training is all from the inside of the airplane, and she knows the jet from the outside. Then he told her his mother had heard about his washout from a lady at church, the day after he'd told her it was going fine, and he asked who would hear it from Kit first. She said Graham first, and then him, if he'd pick up. He wrote his number on her math sheet. Vern had taken most of an hour to find the key to the case, and when he came back she thanked him for the hour and left it there.
Fisk texted for help before his torque retraining at the April drill. She met him at the Riverside and only asked questions, and he worked through the card himself.

The night before the practice test, Graham said he'd call time at the end of every block and say nothing else. Kit went out to the garage for a drill battery. Under the blue tarp behind the mower was a maple crib with an estate sale tag from April 2025, two springs ago, the spring he'd asked her whether this could be the year and she'd said after. She put the tarp back the way it had been. Her own story was coming first, tomorrow night, before she'd ask Graham for his. She stood in the garage until the motion light went off.
Rhonda Shaw. Kit's mother, back from chapter three. She runs a school cafeteria across the river, and she's the only one who calls Kit Kitty.
Saturday, April 3, ten to eight in the morning. Graham had been up since six. Kit could tell by the table.

He'd cleared it down to the wood. Eleven packets sat in a stack at his end, one for each block, a binder clip on every corner and the subtest written across the top in his black marker. He'd put the test together himself over three weeks of nights, out of library books and every practice page he could find, in the order the Pearson page listed and with the minutes it listed. Beside the stack was a coffee mug of sharpened pencils from his classroom, a pad of scratch paper, and the digital timer from his lab with the magnet on the back.
Her coat was on the hook by the door, the sheet still folded in the inside pocket where it had ridden for four weeks.

Graham sat down across from her and slid the first packet over. VERBAL ANALOGIES. He set the timer to eight minutes and pressed the button, and he didn't say go. He'd said what he was going to say on Friday night.
Behind him on the fridge, Saturday's square said PRACTICE TEST, 5 HRS, ME ON THE CLOCK, in green, and under that, small, in his black, 2019.
The analogies went the way they went at Vern's. At eight minutes the timer beeped. Time.

He took the packet, slid the next one over, and set the timer for twenty nine. Arithmetic: pump rates, fuel, a train out of Kansas City, and she was quicker at those than she'd ever been. Then WORD KNOWLEDGE, twenty five in five minutes. Twelve seconds a word.
Number fourteen was DISSEMBLE. She knew the word. She'd known it since high school, and she'd never liked it.

She marked it and went on. To dissemble was to keep a face in front of the truth, and you could do it without saying one false word. She'd stayed for the inspection. Boyd had asked her to. All of it true, and all of it standing in front of a nineteen. She was on fifteen before Graham's timer had moved much.

Dissemble. To hide what's real behind a face, put on a front. Closest in meaning is whichever one fits every place the word goes. It's from the old Latin for disguising yourself, same root as similar. Looking like what you aren't. Then don't trust it to look like its cousins, because one of them is a trap with a wrench in it. Know it, or take your best root guess and get on to the next.
Then MATH KNOWLEDGE, twenty five in twenty two minutes. Graham set the timer and sat back with his coffee. Out the window the neighbor's dog was digging at something by the fence again.

She'd run Vern's four sets on his egg timer, twenty two minutes each, and gone over her misses afterward with no clock at all. She knew where her time went now. At eleven minutes she was on number twelve, about where she wanted to be.
Number fourteen. Circle in a square, and they wanted the corners. She looked at it, and it didn't open.
She put B. It looked about right for corners that size. She circled fourteen on her scratch sheet and went on. Fifteen was a straight line through two points, and she had it in thirty seconds.

That's pace, Sergeant. A guess on the slow one, a mark so you can find it, and on to the next. A guess costs you nothing. A blank never helped anybody. If there's time left over at the end, go back to your circles. The corners are the square less the circle: side squared, minus pi times the radius squared, and the radius is half the side. A side of 10 is 100 less about 78.5, so a little over 21 for all four corners. On Math Knowledge you get about fifty three seconds a problem, and no single problem's worth two of them.
When the timer went she was back on fourteen. The circle had finally opened, and she changed her B to a D with about two seconds left. She didn't know yet whether that was smart.

Reading went by in twenty four minutes. Situational Judgment took thirty five, a stack of young lieutenants with problems that weren't hers, and she found she knew what Vern would say about most of them. Then Graham set the timer for fifteen and pointed at the fridge, which meant food. She ate a sandwich standing up and didn't look at her coat.

Where the inventory went, Graham had left forty five minutes on the clock and nothing to answer, because on the day she'd be that tired. She sat through them with her eyes shut and heard every car go by on Orchard Street.
Then PHYSICAL SCIENCE, twenty in ten minutes. Thirty seconds each. Graham taught this five days a week, and in nine years she'd never once asked him to teach her any of it.

Number six showed two open tanks of water filled to the same depth. One was tall and narrow. The other was as wide as a barn. Graham had drawn them himself, with a little cartoon cow by the wide one. For scale, she guessed.

Neither. It came so fast it surprised her. Out at the dead end of Cooper Road, the pressure was whatever the tower on the hill made it. Not how much water. How high. Two point three one feet to the pound, and she'd done that one at three in the morning more times than she'd ever tell anybody. Marked. Most of her thirty seconds still left for seven.

Depth. And how dense the liquid is. That's all pressure in a liquid cares about. Never width. Wide tank, more water, sure. It's spread over more floor. Each square inch gets the same as the skinny one's. About a pound per square inch every 2.31 feet of fresh water, and you knew that one before I did. The miss is more water, more pressure. I heard a city councilman in Kansas City stand up and argue for a fatter water tower once, to get his ward more pressure. Nobody had the heart.

Then TABLE READING. One grid the size of the whole page. Columns ran minus ten to ten across the top, rows ran ten down to minus ten along the side, plus numbers on top. Forty questions in seven minutes. Graham had run the grid off on the copier in the teachers' lounge, and it had a gray stripe down the middle where the glass was dirty. She put her left hand flat on the table and her pencil in her right.
Number twenty two asked for X minus 4, Y plus 7. She went across the top to minus 4, ran down, and got 63. The choices were 61, 64, 66, 67 and 58. Sixty three wasn't any of them.

She took her pencil back to the edges. X across the top, minus 4. Y down the side, plus 7, up near the top, where Graham had put the plus numbers. She'd run down from the zero row and landed on minus 7. The cell at minus 4, plus 7 said 66, right there in the choices, two over from the 64 she'd almost taken.

When your number isn't there, you slipped. You didn't find a misprint. Go back to the labels, not to the cell you were staring at. X runs across the top, Y down the side, and check which way the side runs, plus at the top or at the bottom. The usual slips are a swapped X and Y, and a lost minus sign. Accuracy first. On this subtest you get about ten seconds a question, and that's enough to find a cell twice.

Instrument Comprehension came and went in five minutes, the dials she'd frozen on in 2019, and she didn't freeze. She didn't do well, either, and she knew it as she went. Block Counting, then Aviation Information, and a little before noon Graham said it for the last time.

He squared the eleven packets into a pile, took the binder clips off and put them in his shirt pocket, and slid the stack into his school bag. Then he kissed the top of her head and went out to mow the side yard, which didn't need it.
She slept two hours on the couch. At six she made eggs, because eggs were what they had, and when the plates were in the sink she went to the hook by the door and took the sheet out of her coat.

She unfolded it on the kitchen table, under the light, where she'd taken the test that morning. Pilot 19. Under it, in Vern's capitals, ACUITY. Graham sat down across from her, in the same chair he'd timed her from, and waited.

It wasn't Boyd. The scores came back that fall, and Pilot was nineteen, and it has to be twenty five. Then Boyd asked me to stay for the inspection, and I said yes. Yes meant I never had to say nineteen to you. I told you he'd asked, and I let that be the reason. She stopped there. She'd thought there would be more, something about being twenty five, and there wasn't.

For a long time Graham didn't say anything. He picked up the sheet and read it again, all the way to the bottom, same as he'd read a lab report. Then he put one finger on the word in the margin, the way he'd point at a wrong answer, only gentler. Whose writing is that? It isn't yours.
Vern's. It's his word, and it's his to tell. He nodded as if that was the one fair thing on the table, and he set the sheet down square with the edge.
In January, when you told me you wanted it, I took a minute before I said okay. You noticed. I was doing some math of my own. I'd made my peace with the slot before I opened my mouth.
I've had three weeks to guess what that 2019 was. I didn't guess this. It's not the slot. You let me think it was Boyd for seven years.
He looked at the dark window over the sink. I used to hold it against him a little. Every Christmas party. There's the guy.

I did. She didn't add the part about the inspection being real. She didn't get up. He looked at the window. She let him. The clock over the stove was loud enough to count. After a while he said Boyd's name once more, not to her, and shook his head.
Near ten he got up, turned on the side light, and stood at the back door with his hand on the knob. Come out to the garage a minute.
Friday she'd put the tarp back the way it had been, and left it for him to lift.

The motion light came on over them. He went past the mower to the back wall and took hold of the corner of the blue tarp, and before he could lift it, she said it. I saw it Friday, when I came out for the battery. I put the tarp back.
He lifted the corner anyway and folded it back over the top rail, and the crib stood there in the light with its paper tag still tied to the post.

Two springs ago I stood right there in that door and asked you if this was the year we tried for a baby. You said after the KC-46 talk. That Saturday there was an estate sale out on Mill Road. Forty dollars. I didn't even haggle.
After your degree. After the inspection. After the deployment. After the new jets. He stopped on the second one. The inspection was the lie too.
It wasn't a question, and she didn't make him ask it. Yes.
I'm not asking you for an answer tonight. I'm asking you not to hand me another after.

I don't know yet. I want to fly, Graham. I don't know how this fits next to that, and I'm not going to put a word on it to make tonight easier. He looked at the crib a while. Okay. No beat in front of it, and no after behind it. He put the tarp corner back where it had been, and on the way out he switched off the light by the door, though it would've gone off by itself.
Sunday morning the 2019 was gone off the whiteboard. There was a gray smear in Saturday's square where a thumb had been, and the green around it was left alone.

Graham went to the hardware store at nine and came back at noon with a box of deck screws and nothing else. He was kind to her all morning, careful about it, the way people are kind in a hospital hallway.
Her mother had texted Saturday afternoon. Kit read it again after lunch, on the back step.
A text from Rhonda. How did the big practice test go Kitty?? Darlene says five hours is longer than her wedding. Call me
Rhonda still had the Boyd version. She'd had it for seven years, and she'd told it at her own table, proud of a daughter who stayed for her people. Boyd was next, at drill.

She called. Rhonda picked up on the first ring, the way she always did, as if she'd had the phone in her hand the whole time. It went fine, Mom. Long. I'll have the numbers this week. Then, before she could talk herself out of it: Can I come by next Sunday, when drill lets out? About four. There's something from 2019 I should've told you. I want to say it at your table. The line went quiet. Is it bad? It's old. Then I'll make a roast, her mother said, and Kit laughed for the first time since Friday.
Tuesday at Vern's she said it with her coat still on. Graham knows. Vern looked at her over the percolator. The index card still stood against it, where it had stood for four weeks.
That's one. He didn't ask how it went. At the end of the night he handed her the week's log, and she read it at the stop sign by the grain elevator with the dome light on.

My log, twenty two January, oh one. Minus eighteen Celsius on the ramp. Trucks metered twenty thousand gallons. Gauges said one hundred thirty eight thousand pounds. The same gallons in August made one thirty two. Did not argue with the gauges.

Graham had put it on the whiteboard back in February, before any of this, one of her blue blocks: WED, MY LAB, 3:30. She hadn't known if it still stood, and she'd decided she wouldn't ask. At three on Wednesday he texted her the room number, as if she might not know it.

Room 114 smelled like the gas taps and a hundred sophomores. He'd set up three stations down the long black bench and pulled a stool up to the first one for her. His school bag was on the floor by his desk, and she could see her eleven packets in it under a stack of lab reports. He hadn't scored them.

He saw her see the bag. Third period took a unit test Monday. Eleven of them came in under half. He was setting two cylinders out on the bench and didn't look up from them. Some of them cried. Then they came in at lunch and we went through it, one at a time. You could've brought me a nineteen. She nodded. Then she showed him Vern's log, because it was what she'd brought.
He read it and handed it back. Your navigator didn't argue with the gauges. Good for him. Same gallons, six thousand more pounds. Where did they come from?

She said it the way she'd have said it on the ramp. Same stuff, packed tighter. Graham nodded once. He got a bottle of cooking oil out of the lab fridge and warmed half of it on the hot plate, and she watched him measure a hundred milliliters of each, slower than he needed to. On the balance the cold one came out about three grams heavier. She thought of the hose in January, so cold it bit through her gloves. Density. Nobody added any fuel. Same fuel, smaller space.

Station two was a pair of plastic syringes with a foot of clear tubing between them and blue water through the whole thing. The skinny one was what you'd use to get a pill into a cat. The fat one she could've stuck her thumb in. Masking tape on each in his printing, 1 SQ CM and 5 SQ CM, on straight, which with Graham meant he'd had time on his hands. He hadn't said her name once since three thirty.

Your truck's brakes. You push a little piston at the pedal, and there's a fat one out at every wheel, with brake fluid between. The jet's the same, except a pump does your pushing, and you'd know how loud. He put two fingers on the skinny one. Say I push this one in ten centimeters with twenty newtons. What's the fat one do?

Twenty newtons on one square centimeter, and that same squeeze all through the blue water. The fat one had five square centimeters for it to push on, so a hundred newtons. A fifth as far. It climbed two centimeters, right on the mark, and the blue in the tube shivered. He worked it on a paper towel from the dispenser with a ballpoint, which tore it. A hundred times two. Twenty times ten. Same work, both ends of the tube. Water doesn't give you anything for free.

That's Pascal. Squeeze a shut in fluid anywhere and you've squeezed it everywhere, same amount. Pressure's force over area. Fat piston, five times the area, five times the shove. And it goes a fifth as far. That's the bill. It always comes. Folks grab the force and forget the bill. Two two eight's gear comes up on that rule every flight. Has since Kennedy. Works because water hardly squeezes. Put a bubble in the line and you're pushing on a sponge, and you know that better than I do.

Station three was the one he liked, she could tell. Plywood, a battery pack out of the supply closet, two bulbs in screw sockets, red and black clip leads all over. Somebody'd written 12 V on the pack in Sharpie, and somebody else had added a smiley face. Gum under the bench lip, gray and old. She'd have bet a week's pay he knew whose.

Call each bulb six ohms. Close enough for government work. Side by side, each one with its own road home. That's parallel. Last clip, and both bulbs lit up hard enough to make her squint. So. How much current's coming out of that battery?

Each road got the whole twelve volts, so two amps a road, and two roads. Graham unclipped one bulb. The other one didn't so much as flicker. She kept her eyes on the one still lit. That's your house, more or less. Every outlet gets the full hundred and twenty. The toaster doesn't care if the lamp's on.

That's parallel, and he set it up so you'd see it. Each branch gets all twelve volts, so you work them one at a time with Ohm's law and add. Twelve over six is two, and two branches makes four. Taken together the two bulbs come out three ohms, lower than either one, since there's a second road now. I sat on the Kansas City beltway enough evenings to know what one more lane does at five o'clock. If you got twelve, you added six and six. That's series, one road through both, one amp, and a couple of dim orange bulbs.
Friday morning she came off nights at ten after seven. The house was empty. Graham had left for school.

The coffee was on, the pot about half full and starting to smell burnt, which meant he'd made it for her and not for himself. On the kitchen table, squared to the edge, were her eleven packets, every page marked in his red pen. Sometime after she'd left for the plant last night, he'd sat down at this table and done all of it.
On the top packet was a yellow sticky note in his printing.
A R, twenty one out of twenty five. Good.
Under it, on the cover page, he'd written every block's number in a column, the way he wrote grades in his book.

Verbal Analogies, twenty of twenty five. Arithmetic Reasoning, twenty one of twenty five. Word Knowledge, nineteen of twenty five. Math Knowledge, twenty of twenty five. Reading, twenty of twenty five. Situational Judgment, twenty five of thirty two. Physical Science, thirteen of twenty. Table Reading, thirty three of forty. Instrument Comprehension, fourteen of twenty five. Block Counting, twenty two of thirty. Aviation Information, eleven of twenty.

She got a pen and went down the cover page against the four that Pilot leans on. Math Knowledge, Table Reading, Instrument Comprehension, Aviation Information. Table Reading was fine. Math she already knew about. Instruments was fourteen of twenty five, and Aviation was eleven of twenty, on a jet she'd been crewing since she was twenty two. She opened the Aviation packet to see what she'd missed, and it was all from inside the airplane, every miss a thing a pilot would know and a crew chief wouldn't. She wrote IC and AI at the top of a clean page and boxed them twice.

Read a practice score where it counts. Pilot leans on Math Knowledge, Table Reading, Instrument Comprehension and Aviation Information, so those four tell you the most about the composite you need. Then open a low one and look for the pattern in the misses. Real percentiles come only from the real test, so don't try to turn raw numbers into one. Physical Science feeds no composite in the 2015 pamphlet. Work on it, but not first.
She read the sticky note again. AR 21/25. Good.

Graham wrote Good on a lab report when it was true. Not once when it wasn't. His sophomores had that figured out by October, and the smart ones by the second week. Every page of eleven packets, marked, at the same table she'd told him at. And the only word on any of it that wasn't a number was that one. Under the one block that earned it.
She read it a third time and still couldn't tell which part of the week it sat under.

She peeled the note off the packet and a little of the cover page came along. She thumbed it flat. Her coat was on the hook. In the inside pocket, same as always, the sheet, folded under Vern's two logs, ACUITY on the inside where nobody'd see it. She stuck Graham's yellow note on the outside of the fold. Next time that sheet came out of her pocket, his note would come out first.
She tore a sheet off his pad of yellow notes and wrote one of her own, in her printing, which was worse than his.
P S, thirteen out of twenty. Will you teach me the seven?

She stuck it on the coffee maker, over the switch. He'd be home at four and she'd be asleep, so he'd find it before he found her. She shut the pot off and poured what was left into the mug with the chipped handle. Six o'clock coffee at a quarter to eight. She drank it anyway, at the sink, boots still on.
